<reason>Side B built a stronger path to victory by exposing internal contradictions in Side A's case—particularly the tension between claiming landlords can unilaterally erase complaint records versus being helpless victims of tenant extortion, and A's clarification/retraction regarding the rent-increase argument. B effectively rebutted the vagueness objection by analogizing to existing housing law standards ("material defect"), defended the disclosure mechanism against perverse-incentive claims by noting tenants control the digital paper trail, and maintained a consistent economic argument that disclosure creates a "lemons discount" that incentivizes repairs over concealment. While A offered plausible concerns about litigation risk and regulatory vagueness, these were undermined by contradictory claims and concessions in Rebuttal 2.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's Rebuttal 2 (Turn 7) decisively exposed the contradiction between A's claims that landlords are vulnerable to tenant extortion [A2.1] versus their power to erase records [A2.2], and seized on A's clarification in [A4.2] to lock in the economic argument that disclosure forces a value-discount that makes fixing defects cheaper than hiding them.</best_rebuttal>
